ta-l1d19q5-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph introducing, with respect to Lombard's second proof (from truth), three articles: what truth is, whether all things are true by one truth, the uncreated or first truth, and the conditions of truth, its eternity and immutability.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3510.summary: First argument that truth is the same as essence. Augustine says the true is that which is, and others say the true is the undividedness of being and that which is. So each thing is called true insofar as it has being, which is the act of essence, and since each thing is formally true by truth, truth and essence are wholly the same.
claims: The true is that which is.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3513.summary: Second argument. Whatever differs really or conceptually can be understood without the other, as God can be understood without understanding his goodness (Boethius), but a thing's essence cannot be understood without truth.
claims: Essence cannot be understood without truth.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3516.summary: Third argument. Whatever differs conceptually from being adds to it, and what adds to something contracts and determines it, as 'man' does 'animal'. Since 'true' does not contract being, the two being convertible, truth differs from essence neither really nor conceptually.
claims: What adds to being contracts it.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3520.summary: Fourth argument from Anselm's definition: truth is rectitude perceptible by the mind alone. He speaks metaphorically, since rectitude properly is a property of the continuous. Goodness and justice by their proper concepts are rectitude perceptible by the mind alone, so truth is the same as goodness and justice really and conceptually.
claims: Anselm defines truth as rectitude perceptible by mind alone.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3523.summary: Sed contra. Something true can be said both of being and of non-being, and non-beings have no essence. Since everything true is true by truth, truth is not the same as essence.
claims: Truths can be stated of non-beings.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3526.summary: Second sed contra. Truth is perceptible by the mind alone (Anselm), so it is not in sensible things but only in intelligible ones, while essence is in both.
claims: Truth is perceived by mind alone.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3529.summary: Third sed contra. Truth and falsity are only in complexes, since no incomplex is true or false, and essence belongs to incomplex things.
claims: Truth and falsity are in complexes only.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3532.summary: Fourth sed contra. Falsity is opposed to truth and is found in beings, as we speak of false gold, but non-being is not said of being. So the false is not the same as non-being, and truth is not the same as essence.
claims: Falsity exists in beings, unlike non-being.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3535.summary: Thomas's determination. What names signify is of three kinds. Some things exist wholly and completely outside the soul, like a man or a stone. Some have nothing outside the soul, like dreams or the image of a chimera. Some have a foundation in the thing outside the soul but are completed in their formal character by the soul's operation, as the universal: humanity is something in the thing but is not universal there, since there is no humanity outside the soul common to many, but as grasped by the intellect an intention is joined to it by which it is called a species. Likewise time is founded in motion's before and after, while its formal element, numbering, is completed by the numbering intellect. Truth too is founded in the thing, but its character is completed by the intellect's action when the thing is grasped as it is, so truth and falsity are in the soul and good and evil in things (the Philosopher). Since a thing has its quiddity and its being, truth is founded more on the thing's being than on its quiddity, as 'being' (ens) is named from esse. In the act of the intellect grasping the thing's being as it is, by assimilation to it, the relation of adequation in which truth consists is completed. So the thing's being is the cause of truth as it is in the intellect's knowledge, but the character of truth is found first in the intellect rather than in the thing, as 'healthy' is said first of the animal and of food and urine by analogy as cause and sign. So 'true' is said first of the intellect's truth, of the statement as its sign, and of the thing as its cause. A thing is called true when it is apt to produce of itself a true apprehension of what appears outwardly in it, and false when apt to produce a false one, as brass is called false gold. A person is false who shows by words or deeds something other than what they are, and by opposition there is truth as a virtue in words and deeds. Both the truth of the intellect and of the thing reduce to God as first principle, since his being causes all being and his understanding all knowledge, so he is first truth as he is first being; each thing stands to truth as to being. The truth of statements reduces to self-evident first principles as first causes, especially that affirmation and negation are not simultaneously true (Avicenna). This explains the different definitions of truth: some by its completion in the intellect's manifestation (Augustine: truth is that by which what is is shown; Hilary: the true is declarative or manifestative of being); some by its foundation in the thing (Augustine: the true is that which is; the schoolmen: the undividedness of being and that which is; Avicenna: the property of each thing's being established for it); some by the commensuration of intellect and thing (truth is the adequation of thing and intellect; Augustine: the true is what is as it appears to a knower who wills and can know); one by appropriation to the Son (Augustine: truth is the supreme likeness of the principle, without any unlikeness); and Anselm's, which covers all: rectitude perceptible by the mind alone, where rectitude touches commensuration and 'perceptible by the mind alone' touches what completes truth. So truth adds to essence conceptually, namely an ordering to knowledge or manifestation.
claims: Truth is founded in the thing's being and completed in the intellect's adequation to it.
'True' is said first of the intellect, then of statements as signs and things as causes.
God is first truth as first being; statements' truth reduces to self-evident first principles.
The various definitions of truth correspond to its foundation, completion, commensuration, and appropriation.
Truth adds to essence conceptually an ordering to knowledge.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3561.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Being' is said in two ways: as signifying the essence of things divided by the ten categories, and as signifying the composition the soul makes, which the Philosopher calls the true. Augustine's 'the true is that which is' means it is true when said of what is, and similarly 'the undividedness of being and that which is'. Though there is truth in negatives, which lies not in composition but division, negative truth is founded on affirmative truth, since no negative is proved except through some affirmative. Alternatively, these definitions concern not the complete character of truth but what is founded in the thing.
claims: 'Being' as composition of the soul is the true; negative truth is founded on affirmative.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3564.summary: Reply to the second argument. As goodness signifies the character by which essence is ordered to appetite, truth signifies the character by which it is ordered to intellect. As no being is desired without the character of good, none is understood without the character of true. Still, the concepts of true and being differ. Something is said not to be understandable without another in two ways: either one cannot be understood unless the other is posited as existing, and in this sense being cannot be understood without the true, as without being intelligible; or whenever one is understood the other is understood, as whoever understands man understands animal. In this sense being can be understood without the true, but not conversely, since the true is not in the concept of being but being is in the concept of the true. One can understand being without understanding intelligibility, but never the intelligible without understanding being. So being is the first conception of the intellect.
claims: Truth orders essence to intellect as goodness orders it to appetite.
Being is in the concept of the true but not conversely; being is the first conception of the intellect.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3567.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'True' adds to being, as 'good' and 'one' do, but none adds a difference contracting being, only a concept following all being: one adds undividedness, good the character of end, and true the ordering to knowledge. So these four, being, good, one, and true, are convertible.
claims: One, true, and good add to being concepts that follow all being without contracting it.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3570.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Rectitude is said metaphorically of goodness, justice, and truth in different senses. In the straight there is an equal proportion of beginning, middle, and end. When someone in distributing or communicating keeps the measure of justice's equality or of the law's precept, there is rectitude of justice; when something does not depart from commensuration with the end, rectitude of goodness; when it does not depart from the order of commensuration of thing and intellect, rectitude of truth.
claims: Rectitude of truth, goodness, and justice differ by what is commensurated.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3573.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. According to Avicenna, nothing can be stated of what in no way exists, since what something is stated of must at least be apprehended and so have some being in the apprehending intellect. So some being always corresponds to truth, though not necessarily being in the thing outside the soul, since truth is completed in the soul.
claims: Some being, at least in the intellect, always corresponds to truth.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3576.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Although being is in sensible things, the senses do not grasp the concept of being or the intention of being, as they grasp no substantial form except per accidens, only sensible accidents. So although truth is in sensible things, as truth in things, the intention of truth is perceived by the intellect alone. Alternatively, though sensible things are grasped by sense, their adequation to intellect is grasped by the mind alone, which is why truth is called perceptible by the mind alone.
claims: The intention of truth, like that of being, is grasped by intellect, not sense.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3580.summary: Reply to the third sed contra. The intellect has two operations: one some call the imagination of the intellect, which the Philosopher calls the understanding of indivisibles, the apprehension of simple quiddity, also called formation; the other they call belief, which consists in composing or dividing a proposition. The first regards a thing's quiddity, the second its being. Since truth is founded on being, not quiddity, truth and falsity are properly in the second operation and its sign, the statement, and only in a qualified way in the first and its sign, the definition, since a quiddity's being is a kind of being of reason, and in this sense a definition is called true. Falsity does not attach per se to this first truth, since the intellect judges truly of its proper object, quiddity, as sight of colour, but per accidens through an attached affirmation or negation. This happens when a definition is compared to something else, as the circle's definition is false of a triangle, or when its parts imply an impossible affirmation, as 'a place in which there is no body' for the void, which is false simply (Metaphysics 5); this occurs only in quiddities of composites, since about simple quiddities the intellect fails only by not understanding at all (Metaphysics 9). Falsity attaches to the second operation per se, not as to the first naturally known affirmations, the axioms, but as to what follows, since in reasoning one can err by applying one thing to another. So the true properly, found only in complexes, does not prevent the convertibility of true and being, since every incomplex thing has its being, which the intellect grasps only by way of composition. From the very concept that 'true' adds to being, ordering to intellect, follows this difference: the true belongs to complexes, while being is said of the incomplex thing outside the soul.
claims: Truth is properly in the second operation (judgment), which regards being, and only in a qualified sense in the first (apprehension of quiddity).
The intellect does not err per se about simple quiddities or first axioms.
The truth of complexes is compatible with the convertibility of true and being.
concepts: falsity per se and per accidens

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3583.summary: Reply to the last sed contra. Being is the intellect's first conception, so nothing can be opposed to it by contrariety or privation, only by negation: as it is founded on nothing, neither is its opposite, since opposites concern the same subject. One, true, and good by their proper intentions are founded on the intention of being and so can have opposites by contrariety or privation founded on being. So true and false, good and evil, do not relate as being and non-being, unless non-being is taken particularly as the removal of something with an underlying being. As every privation of particular being is founded in some good, the false is founded in some truth as in some being. So what has falsity or evil is a being, though not a complete being, and what is evil or false is an incomplete good or truth.
claims: Being has only a negative opposite; true and good have privative opposites founded on being.
The false and the evil are incomplete truth and goodness.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3595.summary: First argument that all things are true by one truth, the uncreated truth. 'True' is said analogically of things in which truth is, as 'healthy' of all healthy things. There is numerically one health from which the animal is called healthy as subject, medicine as cause, and urine as sign. So one truth makes all things true.
claims: Analogical terms like 'healthy' refer to one numerical health.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3598.summary: Second argument. All rectitude is measured by some measure, and truth is a rectitude. As one time measures all temporal things, one truth would measure all true things.
claims: One time measures all temporal things.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3601.summary: Third argument. Truth is to true things as goodness to good things, and all things are good by one goodness: Augustine says, take away this good and that, and you will see the good of every good. So numerically one goodness is participated in all, and likewise all things are true by one uncreated truth.
claims: Augustine: remove this and that good and see the good of every good.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3608.summary: Anticipates the reply that all things are true by uncreated truth as exemplar. The exemplar of every form is in God, the creating essence. If this sufficed for all things to be called true by uncreated truth, all things could also be called coloured by the colour exemplarily in God, which is absurd.
claims: Exemplarity would equally make things coloured by God's colour.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3611.summary: Sed contra. That evils occur is true, but no evil is from God, so not all true things are true by uncreated truth.
claims: No evil is from God.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3614.summary: Thomas's determination. The character of truth consists in two things: the thing's being and the cognitive power's apprehension proportioned to it. Both reduce to God as efficient and exemplar cause, yet each thing participates its own created being, by which it formally is, and each intellect participates the light by which it judges rightly of things, modelled on uncreated light. The intellect also has its own operation, by which truth is completed. So as there is one divine being by which all things are, as by an efficient exemplar principle, while different things have different beings by which they formally are, there is one truth, the divine, by which all things are true as by an efficient exemplar principle, and yet there are many truths in created things by which they are formally true.
claims: All things are true by one divine truth as efficient and exemplar principle, but by many created truths formally.
As with being, truth is one in its source and many in its participants.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3617.summary: Reply to the first argument. Something is said by analogy in three ways. (1) By intention only, not by being: one intention is referred to many by priority and posteriority but has being in only one, as health is referred to animal, urine, and diet but exists only in the animal. (2) By being, not intention: many are equal in a common intention whose being is not of one character in all, as all bodies are equal in the intention of corporeity, so the logician says 'body' is predicated univocally, though the nature's being differs in corruptible and incorruptible bodies, and for the metaphysician and natural philosopher nothing is said univocally of these (Metaphysics 10). (3) By both intention and being: neither the intention nor the being is equal, as 'being' is said of substance and accident, and the common nature must have some being in each, differing by greater or lesser perfection. Truth, goodness, and the like are said analogically of God and creatures in this third way, so they exist in God and creatures by their being, with greater and lesser perfection, and since they cannot be by one being in both, there are diverse truths.
claims: Analogy can be by intention only, by being only, or by both.
Truth is said of God and creatures by analogy of both intention and being, so there are many truths.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3620.summary: Reply to the second argument. Since truth is a rectitude and commensuration, the concept of truth involves a measure, and the commensuration of thing to intellect completes it. Things relate differently to different intellects. The divine intellect is the cause of things, so things are measured by it, each being measured by its first principle; so Anselm says a thing is true when it fulfils what it is ordered to in the divine intellect. Things relate to our intellect as cause, since our intellect receives from them, so our knowledge does not measure things but is measured by them (Metaphysics 10): it is not so in the thing because it seems so to us, but because it is so in the thing, what seems to us is true. So the divine intellect is the first, unmeasured measure; the thing is a second, measured measure; and our intellect is measured and not measuring. The first measure of truth is one, but the second measures, the things themselves, are many, so there are many truths. Even with one measure there would not be only one truth, since truth is not the measure but commensuration or adequation, and there can be different commensurations to one measure in different things. So it is not like time, which is the measure itself.
claims: The divine intellect is the unmeasured measure, things are measured measures, and our intellect is measured only.
There are many truths because truth is the adequation to the measure, not the measure itself.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3623.summary: Reply to the third argument. Likewise there is one goodness by which all things are good as by an efficient exemplar principle, but the goodness by which each is formally good differs in different things. Since universal goodness is found in no creature, only particularized goodness, Augustine says that if we remove all particularizations from goodness, there remains in the intellect whole and full goodness, the divine goodness, seen in created goodness as exemplar in exemplified.
claims: Divine goodness is seen in created goodness as exemplar in exemplified, when particularization is removed.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3627.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The exemplar of things is in God in two ways. In his intellect, as by ideas the divine intellect is the exemplar of everything from it, as an artisan's intellect is of artifacts through the form of the art. In his nature, as by the goodness by which he is good he is the exemplar of all goodness, and likewise of truth. So God is not the exemplar of colour and of truth in the same way, and the objection fails.
claims: God is exemplar by his ideas of all things and by his nature of perfections like goodness and truth.
concepts: exemplarity by ideas vs. by nature

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3630.summary: Reply to the sed contra. Although evil is not good and not from God, understanding evil is good and from God. So the truth that consists in the intellect's commensuration to a privation existing outside the soul is good and from God, which is why Ambrose says every truth, by whomever spoken, is from the Holy Spirit.
claims: Truth about evil is good and from God; every truth is from the Holy Spirit.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3642.summary: First argument that there are several eternal truths. Different propositions have different truths, and 'the Father is God' and 'the Son is God' are two propositions, both true from eternity.
claims: Different propositions have different truths.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3645.summary: Second argument. God foreknew from eternity all that was, is, and will be, which are many, and he foreknew only what is true, so many true things are from eternity.
claims: God foreknew many truths from eternity.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3648.summary: Third argument. Augustine proves the soul's immortality from its being the subject of eternal truth, and the truth in our intellect as subject is not the divine truth by essence, so several truths are eternal. That truth is eternal is proved: whatever is posited by its own removal is eternal. If truth does not exist, then 'truth exists' is false, so 'truth does not exist' is true, which is true only by some truth, so some truth exists.
claims: Denying truth posits truth.
Augustine proves the soul's immortality from truth.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3652.summary: Fourth argument. What cannot be thought not to exist is eternal, since whatever can not be can be thought not to be. Truth cannot be thought not to exist, since whatever is understood is understood by a judgment of truth, so the truth in the intellect is eternal and immutable.
claims: Truth cannot be thought not to exist.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3655.summary: Fifth argument, concerning the truth of statements. If it changed or perished, it would be by destruction of the sign or of the thing, and neither works. Even without a sign, it is right that the thing be signified, and the truth of a sign is the rectitude of signification, so the truth would remain without any statement. Nor does it change with the thing: each thing has truth when it fulfils what it is ordered to in the divine mind, and when Socrates stops running, 'Socrates runs' still does what it is ordered to, signifying that Socrates runs.
claims: The truth of a statement depends neither on the sign's existence nor on the thing.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3658.summary: Sixth argument, concerning the truth in things. Augustine says that when a true thing perishes, truth does not perish. The truth of a thing could be destroyed only by the thing's change, so it does not perish.
claims: When the true perishes, truth does not.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3661.summary: Seventh argument. 'Every whole is greater than its part' and many similar truths seem in no way changeable, so there are several eternal, immutable truths.
claims: Axioms seem immutable.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3667.summary: Sed contra. Augustine says true eternity and sole immutability are in God, and God's truth is one, as his essence is.
claims: True eternity and immutability are in God alone.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3670.summary: Thomas's determination. There is only one eternal truth, the divine truth. Since truth is completed in the intellect's action and founded in the thing's being, judgment about truth follows judgment about the thing's being and the intellect. As only one being is eternal, the divine, only one truth is. The same holds of the mutability of truth as of being: only divine being is simply immutable, so only divine truth is simply immutable. The being of some things is mutable by variability, as in contingents, and their truth is mutable and contingent. The being of others is mutable only by vertibility into nothing, if left to themselves, and their truth likewise. So no truth in creatures is necessary. Speaking of truth as completed in the intellect, no intellect is eternal and invariable by nature except the divine. So only the one truth that is in God, and that God is, is eternal and immutable.
claims: There is only one eternal and immutable truth, the divine truth, which is God.
Created truth follows created being and is mutable, either by variability or by vertibility into nothing.
No truth in creatures is necessary of itself.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3674.summary: Reply to the first argument. As the three persons have one essence by which each has being, though there are several properties distinguishing them, none really different from the essence, so there is one truth of the three persons on the side of the thing stated. That there are several true statements comes from our intellect, so the truth in these statements, by which they are formally true, or in our intellect, is not eternal, as neither the propositions nor our intellect are eternal.
claims: The truth of the thing about the persons is one; the plurality of true statements comes from our non-eternal intellect.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3677.summary: Reply to the second argument. The ideal concepts of things in God from eternity are not really other than the divine intellect and essence, so as the truth of the essence is one in reality, so is the truth of all those concepts, multiplied only by relation to different things. This proves not several truths from eternity but one truth of many in concept.
claims: God's ideas are one truth multiplied only conceptually by relation to things.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3680.summary: Reply to the third argument. If there were no soul or created intellect, truth as consisting in the soul's operation would not exist, though it could remain as founded in the thing, and the intention of truth would remain understood in God. Since neither the soul nor any created intellect is eternal, there was no created truth before they existed. To the objection that if truth does not exist then 'truth exists' is false for that time: it does not follow, since when there is no truth there is no falsity either. This absence comes not from a defect in the intentions of truth and falsity but from a defect of that in which truth has being. As universals are called incorruptible and eternal because they are corrupted only per accidens, as to the being they have in another, which can fail, so truth and falsity considered in their intentions are not corrupted per se, only as to the being they have in another. Augustine's proof rests on this: every power that grasps the concept of an intention must be a power not bound to or dependent on the body, since powers impressed in bodily organs, like the senses, grasp not the concept (of man or colour) but only particulars. A power not dependent on the body is incorruptible, so the intellective soul is immortal because it grasps truth. Sensitive powers, though true in their apprehensions, do not grasp the concept of their truth as the intellect does.
claims: Created truth did not exist before created intellects; truth as an intention is corrupted only per accidens.
The soul's grasp of the intention of truth shows it is independent of the body and so immortal.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3683.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Something cannot be thought not to exist in two ways: on the side of what is understood, when it has being in its concept, like God, whose being is his quiddity through which he is understood; or on the side of the understander, as nothing can be understood without an act of understanding, so the act of understanding cannot be understood not to exist. Truth cannot be understood not to exist in both ways, since it includes being in its concept as founded in the thing and the act of intellect as completed in the soul. Yet it does not follow that it is eternal, except on condition that understanding existed from eternity. Though one cannot understand truth not to exist, grasping the intention of truth without grasping being, it is possible that neither this intellect nor the being on which truth is founded exist, as was once the case. Only the truth founded on eternal being and eternal intellect is eternal.
claims: Truth cannot be thought not to exist, but this does not make created truth eternal.
Only truth founded on eternal being and intellect is eternal.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3686.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The truth of a statement can change in both ways: if there were no statement there would be no statement-truth. It is still right that the thing be signified, but that rectitude is only the thing's signifiability, which posits the sign's truth only in potency, not in act. When the thing changes, the statement's truth changes too, so the same proposition can be true at one time and false at another (the Philosopher). A statement can be considered as a thing, and then it has the truth of a thing when it fulfils what it is ordered to in the divine mind, which remains even when the signified thing changes; or as a sign of the thing, and then its truth is its adequation to it. When the thing changes, the sign's adequation to it is removed without any change in the sign, as happens with relations, so the statement's truth does not remain.
claims: A statement's truth as adequation changes with the thing, without change in the sign.
As a thing in itself, a statement retains the truth of a thing.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3689.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. When a true thing perishes, truth perishes as to the being it had in that thing, but the intention of truth can remain with the being it has in another thing or in the soul. If all these were removed, truth would remain only in God. This defect comes to truth not per se but per accidens: destroy first substances and nothing else can remain (the Philosopher), though universals are incorruptible per se.
claims: Truth perishes per accidens with the true thing but remains in other things, souls, and ultimately God.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3693.summary: Reply to the seventh argument. Likewise the truth of necessary propositions can fail per accidens as to the being it has in the soul or in things, if those failed; then those truths would remain only in God, where they are one and the same truth.
claims: Necessary truths remain eternally only in God, where they are one.

ta-l1d19q5-d1e3703.summary: An expositio textus on the rest of Distinction 19. (1) Augustine's argument that if many attributes in the one person of the Father do not make parts, much less do the three persons, seems to argue from the greater, since simplicity seems greater in one person than in two. It is an argument from the lesser: in the Father he takes things conceptually diverse (wisdom, power), while in Father and Son he takes what is conceptually one, the divine nature, which cannot be multiplied even numerically. (2) 'As three statues are called one gold' seems false, since matter, being a part, is not predicated of the composite. This holds in natural things, whose matter is not their whole substance, but not in artifacts, which are in the genus of substance through their matter, artificial forms being accidents (the Commentator). (3) Damascene's 'substance signifies the common and comprehensive species of homoeideous hypostases' means that the common substance in God is like a species gathering individuals, not that there is a species in the divine essence. (4) Things are said to differ in number when one is not another. Numerical diversity in what is numbered simply comes from division of essence, so one individual is not another and nothing numerically the same is in both. Number in the divine persons follows the distinction of relations, which distinguish supposits without dividing the essence, so the Father is not the Son, yet what is in the Father is also in the Son. (5) God is called triune but not triple because triplicity is a proportion under multiplicity, a species of inequality, so where there is triplicity there is inequality.
claims: Number in the persons follows relational distinction, which distinguishes supposits without dividing the essence.
God is not 'triple', since triplicity implies inequality.

ta-l1d19q5-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 5 introduces three articles on truth, the basis of Lombard's second proof: what truth is, whether all things are true by one uncreated truth, and whether truth is eternal and immutable.

ta-l1d19q5-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks what truth is. Thomas places truth among things founded in reality but completed by the intellect, like universals and time. Truth is founded on the thing's being rather than its quiddity and completed in the intellect's adequation to it, so 'true' is said first of the intellect, then of statements as signs and of things as causes. God is first truth as first being. The definitions of truth by Augustine, Hilary, Avicenna, and Anselm correspond to its foundation, completion, commensuration, and appropriation, and truth adds to being only an ordering to knowledge. Being is the first conception, and truth is properly in judgment rather than in the apprehension of quiddity. True and good have privative opposites founded on being, while being has only a negative opposite.
claims: Truth is the adequation of intellect to the thing's being, founded in being and completed in the intellect.
God is first truth; being is the first conception; truth is properly in judgment.

ta-l1d19q5-Dd1e3587.summary: Article 2 asks whether all things are true by one uncreated truth. As with being, all things are true by one divine truth as efficient exemplar principle but by many created truths formally. Truth is said of God and creatures by analogy of both intention and being, the third of three kinds of analogy. The divine intellect is the unmeasured measure, things are measured measures, and our intellect is measured only, and truth is adequation rather than measure. God is exemplar of goodness and truth by his nature and of all things by his ideas, and every truth, even about evil, is from the Holy Spirit.
claims: All things are true by one divine truth as exemplar, and by many created truths formally.
Truth is said of God and creatures by analogy of intention and being.

ta-l1d19q5-Dd1e3634.summary: Article 3 asks whether there are several eternal truths. Thomas holds that there is only one eternal and immutable truth, the divine truth, which is God. Created truth follows created being and intellect and is mutable by variability or by vertibility into nothing, so no created truth is necessary of itself. Plural true propositions about the persons and God's many ideas are one truth in reality. Created truth did not exist before created intellects, and truth considered as an intention is corrupted only per accidens. The soul's grasp of truth shows its immortality. A statement's truth changes with the thing it signifies, and necessary truths remain eternally only in God.
claims: Only divine truth is eternal and immutable; created truths are mutable.
The intellect's grasp of truth shows the soul's immortality.

ta-l1d19q5-Dd1e3698.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 19 explains Augustine's argument a minori for the simplicity of the Trinity, the 'one gold' of three statues, and Damascene's 'species'. It explains that number in the persons follows relational distinction without dividing the essence, and that God is triune but not triple, since triplicity implies inequality.
claims: Number in God distinguishes supposits without dividing the essence.

ta-l1d19q5.summary: Quaestio 5 of Book I, Distinction 19 gives Thomas's theory of truth, as the basis of Lombard's proof of the persons' equality from truth. Article 1 holds that truth is founded in the thing's being and completed in the intellect's adequation to it, so it is found first in the intellect, especially in judgment, and secondarily in statements and things. God is first truth as first being, and being is the intellect's first conception, with truth adding only an ordering to knowledge. Article 2 holds that all things are true by one divine truth as efficient exemplar principle and by many created truths formally, truth being said analogically by both intention and being, with the divine intellect as unmeasured measure. Article 3 holds that only divine truth is eternal and immutable. Created truth is mutable, the soul's grasp of truth proves its immortality, and necessary truths are eternal only in God.
claims: Truth is the adequation of intellect and thing, founded on being and completed in judgment.
All things are true by one divine truth as exemplar and by many created truths formally.
Only divine truth is eternal; created truths are mutable.
